questions.q: Why might a pretrained base model respond poorly to a direct question, even though it was trained on vast amounts of text containing questions and answers?
options: Its training objective is next-token completion in whatever style the prompt implies, with no built-in notion that a prompt is an instruction requiring a direct, helpful response
Base models are only trained on non-English text
Base models cannot process questions at all
Questions are always removed from pretraining corpora
questions.explain: A base model simply continues text plausibly given its training distribution; it has no inherent concept of 'this is an instruction, now answer helpfully' until that behavior is taught via instruction tuning.

questions.q: In instruction tuning, how is the loss typically computed over a training example?
options: Only over the first token of the response
Over the entire prompt and response combined, weighted equally
Loss is not used during instruction tuning
Over the response tokens only, with the instruction/prompt tokens present as context but usually masked out of the loss
questions.explain: The training objective remains next-token prediction, but cross-entropy loss is typically computed only over the response tokens, with the prompt masked out, a detail covered further in Lesson 23.

questions.q: Why does a comparatively small instruction-tuning dataset produce such a large behavioral shift, compared to the trillions of pretraining tokens?
options: Because pretraining has already built most of the underlying knowledge and capability; instruction tuning mainly teaches the model which existing capability to use by demonstration, rather than injecting new knowledge
Because instruction tuning uses a completely different neural network architecture
Because base models have no knowledge at all before instruction tuning
Because instruction-tuning data is weighted a million times more heavily in the loss function
questions.explain: The widely accepted explanation is that SFT elicits and reweights capability already latent from pretraining rather than teaching new facts, which is why relatively little data produces a large behavioral change.

questions.q: What did Google's FLAN paper (Wei et al., 2021) demonstrate?
options: That larger pretraining corpora eliminate the need for fine-tuning
That fine-tuning on a large collection of NLP tasks phrased as instructions dramatically improved zero-shot performance on held-out tasks never seen during instruction tuning
That instruction tuning requires more data than pretraining
That reinforcement learning alone is sufficient for instruction following
questions.explain: FLAN showed that instruction-tuning on a diverse set of tasks framed as instructions generalized well to new, unseen tasks in a zero-shot setting.

questions.q: How does instruction tuning (SFT) differ from the preference-tuning stage (RLHF/DPO) that typically follows it?
options: Preference tuning always comes before SFT
SFT teaches the model to produce a good response in a demonstrated style; preference tuning teaches the model to compare multiple plausible responses and prefer the better one
SFT and preference tuning are the exact same process with different names
SFT requires no training data at all
questions.explain: SFT establishes reasonable, on-distribution responses via demonstration. Preference-tuning methods like RLHF or DPO then add comparative judgment -- choosing between multiple candidate responses -- which SFT alone does not teach.
